myths.title: The "Viking compass" that isn’t
myths.claim: The Vegvísir — the eight-armed stave in a thousand tattoos — is an ancient Viking symbol carried for guidance.
myths.verdict: It appears first in a 17th-century Icelandic manuscript (the Huld manuscript, c. 1860 in its surviving copy) — roughly six hundred years after the Viking Age ended. No Vegvísir is carved, written, or described in any Viking-Age source.
myths.correct: Ink it if you love it — but ink it as an early-modern Icelandic magical stave, not as something a Viking would recognize. If you want a genuinely Viking-Age mark, use an attested runic inscription.

myths.title: Viking names in the wrong runes
myths.claim: Tattoo shops write Þórr, Óðinn and Freyja in the Elder Futhark — the 24-rune alphabet all over the internet.
myths.verdict: The Elder Futhark was largely out of use by c. 700 CE — before the Viking Age began. Vikings carved the 16-rune Younger Futhark: Þórr is ᚦᚢᚱ, not ᚦᛟᚱᚱ. An Elder Futhark "Thor" would have looked archaic to a Viking, like Gothic script looks to us.
myths.correct: For any Viking-Age name, use the attested Younger Futhark form — the corpus below carries per-sign provenance for each. Elder Futhark is correct only for names from before c. 700 CE.

myths.title: "Your name" in hieroglyphs
myths.claim: A cartouche generator can write your name in authentic ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs.
myths.verdict: Egyptian writing did not record vowels, and modern names do not exist in ancient Egyptian. Every "your name in hieroglyphs" is a modern phonetic bridge — a scholarly convention, not an attestation. Even for the gods, the vocalization (Ra, Amun, Isis) is conventional: the signs are real, the vowels are ours.
myths.correct: Treat a cartouche as a translation exercise, not an ancient artifact. For god names, use the attested sign groups with their conventional reading clearly labelled — the way this site labels them everywhere.

myths.title: Greek, minus the "squiggles"
myths.claim: Greek looks cleaner without the accents and breathings — Ἀθηνᾶ becomes Αθηνα.
myths.verdict: Two different things are true. Lowercase Greek without breathings and accents is simply misspelled — the marks are part of the letters. But monumental capitals (ΑΘΗΝΑ) are epigraphically legitimate: ancient stone inscriptions were carved in majuscule without those marks.
myths.correct: Choose deliberately. Lowercase: keep every accent and breathing (Ἀθηνᾶ). Monumental capitals are correct in the ancient inscriptional style. Lowercase-without-marks is correct in neither.

myths.title: "Rune of power" meanings, one letter at a time
myths.claim: Each rune carries a fixed mystical meaning, so any word can be "translated" into a power sigil letter by letter.
myths.verdict: Rune poems do give the letters names (cattle, hail, yew) — but they are alphabets first. A modern word spelled into runes is a transcription, not a talisman, and the neat "meanings" tables online mostly descend from 20th-century occultism, not medieval sources.
myths.correct: If you want a word with genuine charge, use a word the sources actually attest — a god’s name in its own script — rather than a letter-by-letter spell of an English word.

signs.name: nichi / hi / hi 'sun'
signs.note: Kanji for 'sun' / 'day'; read nichi in on'yomi, hi in kun'yomi.

signs.name: kō / hikari 'light'
signs.note: Kanji for 'light'; the on'yomi kō supplies the long -ō of Nikkō.

signs.name: fū / kaze 'wind'
signs.note: Kanji for 'wind'; read fū in Sino-Japanese on'yomi, kaze in native kun'yomi.

signs.name: chi / ji 'earth, ground'
signs.note: The left-hand earth radical (土) gives the meaning; the right-hand component supplies the sound.

signs.name: zō 'storehouse, treasury'
signs.note: Combines the grass radical (艹) with 臣 and 戈; denotes a repository, womb, or treasury.

signs.name: Manannán 'son of the sea'
signs.note: The name is traditionally derived from Manann, a figure linked to the Isle of Man; the final -án is a diminutive or patronymic suffix.

signs.name: mac Lir 'son of Lir'
signs.note: Ler / Lir is an old personification of the sea in Irish tradition.
